## TL;DR

Reviewed empty, loading, and error behavior on Agents, Checks, and Releases. The UI already had useful empty and loading states plus retained-data refresh failures. The review found one accessibility inconsistency: initial load errors on Checks and Releases were not announced as alerts even though refresh failures were announced. Both initial errors now use `role="alert"`; a regression assertion also confirms cached Checks refresh failures remain `role="status"`. Focused UI tests passed: 123 tests across five files.

## Work and rationale

I read the task and inspected the three views alongside the existing UI fixture and test coverage. The goal was a QA pass, so I looked for state transitions and whether each state gave a user a clear next step, rather than replacing already useful patterns with new copy or components.

Agents had the most complete coverage already. The `agents:empty` route fixture makes the agent list empty without modifying the saved config and offers a path to built-in agent choices. A separate test holds config loading unresolved and confirms the page title and primary tabs remain visible while the skeleton is shown. Existing model-list and model-test tests cover actionable failures, including retry guidance. This means an empty project remains understandable and can be configured, while model-level failures do not erase the rest of the page.

Checks also separates initial loading from refreshing. A skeleton appears only when a plan is not yet available; an already-loaded plan remains in place during refresh. A genuine zero-step plan receives setup guidance, and the no-run case says there is no recorded run yet. A refresh failure has cached content to work with, so it correctly uses a status announcement. During review I noticed the first-load error branch had no alert role. Since the entire plan could not be loaded in that case, I added `role="alert"` there and strengthened the refresh regression test to preserve the distinct `role="status"` behavior.

Releases explains when release configuration is disabled, shows skeletons for initial status and distribution loading, and retains prior data during refresh failures. The initial status failure similarly had no alert role, despite being the only content explaining why the page is unavailable. I added `role="alert"` to that branch. Refresh errors remain status announcements because the page's previously loaded state is still visible.

I wrote the requested QA findings to `docs/qa/2026-11-empty-error-states-qa.md`. The document records the existing fixture/test evidence, code-level state review, and the limits of this pass.

## Approaches tried

I first searched the UI tests for existing state fixtures and mounted-view tests, then read only the relevant sections of the page implementations. This established that adding duplicate fixtures would create unnecessary parallel state machinery: Agents already had an explicit empty fixture, while Checks and Releases had deterministic view tests that stub success, no-data, and failure responses. I reused that coverage and made only the accessible error-announcement adjustment.

I ran the focused UI test command for the Agents view, Checks page, Releases view, and release status tests. It completed successfully with 123 tests passing across five test files. I then prepared the changed-path RepoOS check required by the task; its final result is reported in the turn handoff.

## Challenges and blockers

The acceptance criteria name explicit viewport widths of 375, 768, and 1280 pixels and require headless Playwright. This managed task-runner session does not allow starting `repoos serve`, and the task did not request a managed preview. I did not open a visible browser or claim that I directly measured screenshots at those widths. The changed-path gate's headless UI smoke passed and reported Checks tabs at 320, 390 and 1440 px in light and dark mode. It did not report Agents and Releases at 375, 768 or 1280 px, so I have not claimed those viewport checks. The QA document states that limit plainly instead of presenting an unobserved result as evidence.

## Key learnings

These pages already had a useful distinction between initial load errors and refresh errors in their copy, but their accessibility semantics were inconsistent. A failed initial load needs an assertive announcement because the page has no usable data; a failed refresh should remain a status update when cached content is still present. Preserving that distinction gives screen-reader users the same context sighted users get from the retained page and error copy.

Fixture evidence should also be described at the level actually exercised. Unit-mounted view tests with controlled fetch responses are good evidence for state transitions and text, but they are not screenshots or viewport measurements. The report and QA note separate those claims so future visual verification can add evidence without having to undo an unsupported assertion.
